guide.title: Architecture overview
guide.purpose: See the main parts of the system, how a request travels from the browser to a workspace container, and which file to open first.
guide.markdown:
OpenCode Multiuser is one FastAPI process that is both a control plane (accounts, workspaces, admin) and a reverse proxy in front of per-workspace OpenCode containers. This page shows the pieces, follows one browser request to a container, and says where to start reading. ## The main parts ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Browser"] --> M["app/main.py
routes + auth"] M --> G["app/gateway.py
proxy_http"] G -->|"Basic Auth, loopback port"| C["OpenCode container"] M --> R["app/runtime.py
start_workspace"] R -->|"podman run"| C M --> D[("Database
app/db.py + models.py")] S["app/config.py
settings"] -.-> M S -.-> G S -.-> R ``` - **Control plane, `app/main.py`.** It creates the FastAPI `app` with the title "OpenCode Multiuser Gateway" and moves the interactive docs under `/_control` [[app/main.py:309-316]]. It holds the login and registration routes, the dashboard, the admin and workspace APIs, and the proxy routes. See [Authentication and roles](wiki:authentication-and-roles) for the sign-in side. - **Gateway, `app/gateway.py`.** `proxy_http` forwards one HTTP request to the user's selected workspace [[app/gateway.py:132-203]]. See [The gateway proxy](wiki:gateway-proxy). - **Runtime, `app/runtime.py`.** `start_workspace` starts one isolated container for a workspace in a given slot and returns once it is healthy [[app/runtime.py:207-266]]. See [Starting a workspace runtime](wiki:starting-a-workspace-runtime). - **Data, `app/models.py` and `app/db.py`.** The models define users, `Slot` rows and `Workspace` rows [[app/models.py:26-57]]. `app/db.py` builds the engine from `settings.database_url` and exposes `get_db`, a per-request session dependency that always closes the session [[app/db.py:14-23]]. Startup creates a partial index over active workspaces (starting, running, stopping) after collapsing duplicates, so the database can enforce one active workspace per user and project [[app/main.py:145-147]]. See [Slots and workspace leases](wiki:slots-and-workspace-leases). - **Configuration, `app/config.py`.** `Settings` is a pydantic-settings model read from environment variables and an optional `.env` file [[app/config.py:5-6]]. Domain and ports, JWT and cookies, local and OIDC authentication, Podman limits and Traefik options all live there [[app/config.py:8-67]]. - **Traefik helpers, `app/traefik.py`.** `workspace_open_url` builds `/open/` [[app/traefik.py:4-5]]. The app no longer uses per-workspace Traefik files; startup removes leftovers from the older design [[app/main.py:292-294]]. What Traefik does in front of the portal is not visible in the files shown here. ## One request, browser to container 1. **Sign in.** `login` checks a local password and `_set_session_cookie` stores a token in the session cookie [[app/main.py:364-381]]. 2. **Start a workspace.** `POST /workspaces/start` takes the first free `Slot`, ordered by id. On non-SQLite databases it locks the row with `skip_locked` so concurrent starts cannot take the same slot [[app/main.py:682-685]]. It marks the slot and workspace as in use, commits, and then calls `start_workspace` [[app/main.py:701-707]]. If the start fails, the slot is released and the workspace is marked `ERROR` [[app/main.py:713-719]]. 3. **Create the container.** `start_workspace` generates a random per-workspace password and writes it to disk [[app/runtime.py:213-219]]. It publishes the container's port 4096 only on `127.0.0.1` at a host port computed from the slot [[app/runtime.py:214-214]]. The base port is the setting `workspace_host_port_base` [[app/config.py:58-58]]. The container also gets that password as `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` [[app/runtime.py:247-247]], memory, CPU and PID limits, dropped capabilities, and a read-only root filesystem [[app/runtime.py:228-234]]. It then waits for readiness, and removes the container if the wait fails [[app/runtime.py:260-264]]. 4. **Select the workspace.** `GET /open/{workspace_id}` accepts only a running workspace owned by the caller. It refuses one with no gateway secret file, stamps activity, and sets the workspace cookie before redirecting to `/` [[app/main.py:829-859]]. 5. **Proxy.** Every other path falls through to a catch-all route, which the source says must stay last so the control-plane endpoints remain local [[app/main.py:946-948]]. It requires `current_user`, resolves the workspace with `selected_workspace_for_request`, and checks `_workspace_runtime_usable` [[app/main.py:948-957]]. A workspace whose container is gone is released and the browser is sent back to the dashboard [[app/main.py:957-967]]. Otherwise the request goes to `proxy_http` [[app/main.py:977-977]]. 6. **Swap credentials and forward.** `proxy_http` records activity, reads the workspace secret, builds the target URL and forwards the request with headers built by `_forward_headers` and the workspace password [[app/gateway.py:133-138]]. The body of `_forward_headers` is not shown here. The response streams back and each chunk refreshes the activity timestamp [[app/gateway.py:168-181]]. A successful HTML response is instead read fully and rewritten to include the portal widget [[app/gateway.py:154-166]]. A connection failure becomes HTTP 502 [[app/gateway.py:146-152]]. WebSockets go through a separate route that hands off to `proxy_websocket`, whose body is not shown [[app/main.py:986-989]]. The browser never sees the workspace password. The portal's session cookie decides who the user is, and the gateway adds the container's own credentials on the way through. ## What happens at startup The `lifespan` context manager validates the auth settings, runs the schema migrations, creates tables, seeds slots, creates the data directories and removes the legacy Traefik routes. It then reconciles database leases with real containers and removes duplicate active workspaces before adding the unique index [[app/main.py:281-297]]. If `workspace_idle_timeout_minutes` is above zero, it also starts a background reaper task and cancels it on shutdown [[app/main.py:298-306]]. The details are in [Startup, reconciliation and idle reclamation](wiki:startup-reconciliation-and-idle-reclamation). ## Where to open first Start with `app/main.py`. Its routes are the table of contents for the whole system, and the proxy routes at the bottom show how everything connects. Then read `app/gateway.py` for the request path, `app/runtime.py` for container creation, and `app/models.py` for the invariants the database enforces. Keep `app/config.py` open beside them: the limits, cookie names, ports and timeouts used above are all `settings` fields.

guide.title: Authentication and roles
guide.purpose: Understand how local and OIDC sign-in produce a session token, how admins are identified, and where authorization is enforced.
guide.markdown:
The portal supports two ways to sign in, a local username and password or an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider. Both end in the same signed session token, and every later authorization decision comes from that token plus the user's row in the database. This page covers how the token is made, how admins are identified, and where access is enforced.

## Two sign-in paths, one token

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    L["POST /auth/login"] --> V["verify_password()"]
    R["POST /auth/register"] --> H["hash_password()"]
    O["GET /auth/oidc/callback"] --> P["provision_oidc_user()"]
    V --> T["issue_token()"]
    H --> T
    P --> T
    T --> K["Session cookie"]
    K --> C["current_user()"]
    C --> A["require_admin()"]
```

`issue_token` signs an HS256 JWT with `settings.jwt_secret`. The payload holds the user id (`sub`), username, role, issue time and an expiry of `jwt_ttl_minutes` [[app/security.py:45-54]], which defaults to 480 [[app/config.py:15-16]]. The token is returned in a `TokenResponse` and also stored in the session cookie through `_set_session_cookie` [[app/main.py:358-360]]. The OIDC callback sets the same cookie but redirects instead of returning JSON [[app/main.py:408-410]]. The body of `_set_session_cookie` is not in the listing for this page.

### Local accounts

`register` refuses when local auth is disabled or registration is closed [[app/main.py:339-342]]. It asks `role_for_new_user` for a role, stores an Argon2 hash from `hash_password`, and turns a duplicate username into HTTP 409 [[app/main.py:343-356]]. Input limits sit in `RegisterRequest`: a username of 3-80 characters matching `[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]` and a password of 12-256 characters [[app/schemas.py:4-6]].

`login` looks only for active users whose `auth_provider` is `local` [[app/main.py:367-373]]. A missing user and a wrong password both give the same 401 "Invalid credentials" [[app/main.py:374-375]]. `verify_password` returns `False` when the account has no hash, so an OIDC account can never match a password [[app/security.py:21-27]]. A successful login updates `last_login_at` before the token is issued [[app/main.py:376-381]].

### OIDC accounts

`oidc_client` raises 404 when OIDC is not configured and 503 when Authlib is missing or the client cannot be created [[app/oidc.py:44-53]]. The Authlib import is wrapped so a local-only install still starts [[app/oidc.py:5-8]]. The provider is registered once, with PKCE (`S256`) when `oidc_use_pkce` is set [[app/oidc.py:23-41]]. `oidc_configured` needs `oidc_enabled`, an issuer and a client id [[app/config.py:95-97]]. The redirect URI defaults to `<control_plane_url>/auth/oidc/callback` [[app/config.py:105-109]].

`oidc_callback` exchanges the code, requires `userinfo` in the token response, and calls `provision_oidc_user` [[app/main.py:392-397]]. Any failure, whether a rejected `HTTPException` or an unexpected error, is logged and answered with a 303 to `/login?error=oidc`, so the browser never sees the cause [[app/main.py:401-406]].

`provision_oidc_user` identifies a person by the pair `(issuer, subject)`, not by username or email. The issuer is stored without a trailing slash [[app/oidc.py:88-95]]. The `User` model backs this with a unique index on `oidc_issuer` and `oidc_subject`, limited to rows where `oidc_subject IS NOT NULL` [[app/models.py:28-37]].

- A matching but disabled account gets 403. An active one has its email and display name refreshed from the claims [[app/oidc.py:96-102]].
- An unknown user is rejected with 403 unless `oidc_auto_provision` is on [[app/oidc.py:104-105]].
- A new user gets `password_hash=None` and `auth_provider="oidc"` [[app/oidc.py:107-117]]. The username comes from the configured claims, falling back to email, name and `sub`, with unsafe characters replaced [[app/oidc.py:64-75]]. If that name is taken, an 8-character hash of issuer and subject is appended [[app/oidc.py:78-84]].
- If two callbacks race, the second commit hits the unique index. The code rolls back and returns the row the other request created [[app/oidc.py:119-129]].

## How admins are identified

Roles are the two values of `UserRole`, `admin` and `developer`; the `role` column defaults to developer [[app/models.py:21-24]]. There is no separate admin table. An administrator is a user whose `role` is `admin`.

The first account ever created becomes the administrator. `role_for_new_user` counts the users and returns `admin` when the count is zero. Otherwise it returns the requested default, falling back to `developer` for an unknown role string [[app/security.py:36-42]]. On PostgreSQL it first takes a `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` lock on `users`, so two simultaneous first registrations cannot both become admin [[app/security.py:30-38]]. The rule applies to both paths: `register` calls it with no argument, and `provision_oidc_user` passes `oidc_default_role` [[app/main.py:343-343]] [[app/oidc.py:107-107]]. A test confirms that the first OIDC login gets `admin` [[tests/test_gateway.py:303-323]].

## Where authorization is enforced

`current_user` is a FastAPI dependency. It takes a bearer token if one is sent (the `OAuth2PasswordBearer` scheme has `auto_error=False`) and otherwise reads the session cookie. It raises 401 when no active user results [[app/security.py:14-14]]. `require_admin` builds on it and raises 403 for any user whose role is not `admin` [[app/security.py:80-83]]. A test checks that an admin passes and a developer gets 403 [[tests/test_gateway.py:345-356]].

`load_user_from_token` does the real work. It decodes only HS256 tokens and treats any decoding error as "no user". It then loads the user by `sub` with `is_active` true [[app/security.py:57-65]]. Two consequences follow from the code:

- The token's `role` claim is not read here. Role comes from the database row on every request, so a demotion takes effect immediately.
- Disabling an account blocks its existing tokens at once, because the active check is part of the lookup.

The shown code keeps no server-side record of issued tokens. `logout` clears the OIDC state session, stops the user's workspaces if `stop_workspaces_on_logout` is set, and deletes the session and workspace cookies [[app/main.py:414-422]]. It does not invalidate a token someone has copied.

The route table is mostly outside this page's listing. The admin endpoints depend on `require_admin` and the workspace and proxy routes on `current_user`; those declarations are not shown here. Admin-only invariants also live in the application code. A test shows that `_protect_last_admin` raises 409 when removing the only enabled administrator and allows it once a second admin exists [[tests/test_gateway.py:359-382]]. Role updates are limited by schema to `admin` or `developer` [[app/schemas.py:33-34]]. See [Admin console and engine updates](wiki:admin-console-and-engine-updates) for those flows.

## Configuration guard

`Settings.validate_auth` fails fast with a `RuntimeError` if neither local auth nor a configured OIDC provider is available, or if `OIDC_ENABLED` is set without an issuer and client id [[app/config.py:111-119]]. Local auth and registration default to on, and OIDC defaults to off, so a fresh install works before any provider exists [[app/config.py:21-25]]. For where this check runs, see [Architecture overview](wiki:architecture-overview).

guide.title: Slots and workspace leases
guide.purpose: Learn how capacity is modelled as slots, how a workspace holds one, and what guarantees the database enforces.
guide.markdown:
Capacity in opencode-multiuser is a fixed pool of numbered slots. A workspace is allowed to run a container only while it holds one, and a small number of database rules keep that bookkeeping consistent. This page covers the tables, how a slot is claimed and returned, and which guarantees come from the database rather than from application code.

## The data model

Two tables carry the lease. `Slot` is one row per unit of capacity: an integer primary key, an indexed `in_use` flag and a nullable `workspace_id` recording the owner [[app/models.py:53-57]]. `Workspace` is a user's workspace for one project. It points back to the slot with a nullable foreign key `slot_id`, and carries `container_name` and a `status` [[app/models.py:60-83]].

The two sides of the lease are therefore stored twice: `Slot.in_use`/`Slot.workspace_id` on the slot, and `Workspace.slot_id` on the workspace. Only the workspace side is a real foreign key; `Slot.workspace_id` is a plain 36-character string column [[app/models.py:55-57]] [[app/models.py:76-76]]. Keeping both in step is the job of the helpers in `app/main.py`.

`WorkspaceStatus` has five states: starting, running, stopping, stopped and error [[app/models.py:13-18]]. Only the first three count as "active", and that distinction is what the database enforces.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> STARTING: slot claimed
    STARTING --> RUNNING: container healthy
    STARTING --> ERROR: start failed
    RUNNING --> STOPPING: release begins
    STARTING --> STOPPING: release begins
    STOPPING --> STOPPED: slot freed
    RUNNING --> STOPPED: release of stale row
    STOPPED --> STARTING: restarted
    ERROR --> STARTING: restarted
```

The transitions come from the start handler [[app/main.py:692-692]] [[app/main.py:709-709]] [[app/main.py:717-717]] and from `_release_workspace` [[app/main.py:86-88]] [[app/main.py:100-100]].

## Seeding the pool

`_seed_slots` makes sure a `Slot` row exists for every id from 1 to `settings.max_slots`, adding only the missing ones [[app/main.py:72-78]]. It runs at startup from `lifespan` [[app/main.py:289-289]]. Because it only adds, lowering `max_slots` later does not remove existing rows. The code shown does not delete them, so the pool can stay larger than the setting.

Slot ids matter beyond bookkeeping: `workspace_host_port` maps a slot id to the loopback port its container is published on, as `workspace_host_port_base + slot_id` [[app/runtime.py:164-165]]. A slot is thus also a port reservation. [Starting a workspace runtime](wiki:starting-a-workspace-runtime) shows where that port is used.

## Claiming a slot

The `/workspaces/start` handler does the claim [[app/main.py:662-719]]:

1. It loads the user's newest workspace row for the project. If that row is STARTING or RUNNING and the runtime looks healthy (secret file present, container running), it just touches the activity timestamp and returns it. Otherwise it releases the stale row first [[app/main.py:664-680]].
2. It selects the lowest-numbered free slot. On any database other than SQLite the query adds `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so concurrent requests lock different rows instead of waiting on or colliding over the same slot [[app/main.py:682-685]].
3. With no free slot it answers 503 "No workspace capacity available" [[app/main.py:686-687]].
4. It reuses the existing row (resetting status, container name and timestamps) or creates a new one, then marks the slot `in_use` with the workspace id, and commits [[app/main.py:689-704]].

The commit in step 4 happens before the container is started. The lease is therefore durable and visible to other requests while the slow container start runs [[app/main.py:703-707]]. If `start_workspace` raises, the handler frees the slot and sets the workspace to ERROR, returning HTTP 500 [[app/main.py:713-719]]. It does not clear `ws.slot_id` on that path, and `stop_workspace(ws.container_name)` sees a `None` name because the name is only assigned after a successful start [[app/main.py:693-693]] [[app/main.py:708-708]] [[app/main.py:714-718]].

## Returning a slot

`_release_workspace` is the single place that undoes a lease. It marks a non-terminal workspace STOPPING and commits, removes the container, clears `in_use` and `workspace_id` on the slot, then sets STOPPED, stamps `stopped_at`, clears `container_name` and `slot_id`, records a stop reason and commits once [[app/main.py:84-105]]. The slot release and the final status change land in the same commit, so they cannot be observed half-done.

Everything that stops work goes through it: the manual stop route [[app/main.py:722-732]], `_stop_user_workspaces` for logout and admin actions [[app/main.py:170-179]] [[app/main.py:417-418]], the idle reaper [[app/main.py:262-262]], and the recycling of runtimes that are no longer usable [[app/main.py:110-118]] [[app/main.py:141-141]]. Those last two are covered in [Startup, reconciliation and idle reclamation](wiki:startup-reconciliation-and-idle-reclamation).

The dashboard derives its capacity numbers straight from the table: total slots and slots where `in_use` is false [[app/main.py:482-484]].

## What the database enforces

The central invariant is one active workspace per user and project. `Workspace` declares a unique index `uq_active_workspace` on `(user_id, project_slug)`, restricted by a `WHERE` clause to rows in STARTING, RUNNING or STOPPING, for both PostgreSQL and SQLite [[app/models.py:62-71]]. STOPPED and ERROR rows are outside the index, so a user can accumulate any number of historical rows for a project but never two live ones. A second concurrent insert for the same pair fails at the database. The start handler shown does not catch that error around its flush or commit [[app/main.py:699-699]] [[app/main.py:703-703]].

A fresh database gets the index from the model. An existing one gets it from `ensure_active_workspace_index`, which runs `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` with the same predicate and skips dialects other than PostgreSQL and SQLite with a warning [[app/migrations.py:95-109]]. That makes it safe to run on every startup.

Older databases might already hold duplicates, which would make index creation fail. `_dedupe_active_workspaces` handles this: it orders active rows by user, project and newest first, keeps the first of each pair and releases the rest [[app/main.py:145-167]]. The startup order is deliberate: reconcile, dedupe, then create the index [[app/main.py:295-297]]. A legacy constraint, `uq_activeish_workspace`, is dropped even earlier, before tables are created [[app/migrations.py:83-92]] [[app/main.py:286-286]].

What the schema does not enforce is slot exclusivity. The code shown has no unique constraint on `Workspace.slot_id` [[app/models.py:76-76]]. Two workspaces never share a slot because the claim path selects only free slots and, on databases other than SQLite, locks the row it picks [[app/main.py:682-685]].

guide.title: Starting a workspace runtime
guide.purpose: See what happens when a container is created: on-disk layout, security flags, the managed provider policy and the readiness wait.
guide.markdown:
A workspace runtime is one locked-down OpenCode container plus a directory tree on the host. This page follows `start_workspace` from the on-disk layout through the container flags and the administrator's provider policy to the readiness wait. The slot it is given is explained in [Slots and workspace leases](wiki:slots-and-workspace-leases). The callers of `start_workspace` are in `app/main.py`, which this page's sources do not include.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant S as start_workspace
    participant D as Host disk
    participant P as Podman
    participant O as OpenCode
    C->>S: user, project, workspace id, slot
    S->>P: ensure network
    S->>D: create dirs, policy file
    S->>P: rm -f old name
    S->>D: write secret
    S->>P: run -d with limits
    loop until healthy or timeout
        S->>O: GET /global/health
    end
    S->>D: touch last-activity
    S-->>C: RuntimeResult
```

## On-disk layout

Everything lives under `settings.expanded_data_root`, which expands `%h` and `~` and resolves the path [[app/config.py:69-71]]; the default is `~/.local/share/opencode-multiuser` [[app/config.py:48-48]]. `workspace_root` returns `<data_root>/users/<user_id>/<project_slug>` [[app/runtime.py:49-52]]. It first validates the slug against `^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$` and explicitly rejects `.` and `..`, so a slug cannot climb out of the user directory [[app/runtime.py:15-15]] [[app/runtime.py:50-51]]. A test checks the dot-segment rejection [[tests/test_gateway.py:114-121]].

`workspace_paths` creates and returns four persistent directories under that root: `workspace`, `opencode-data`, `opencode-state` and `opencode-config` [[app/runtime.py:55-63]]. Next to them sit small files managed by other helpers: `runtime-secret`, `last-activity` and `stop-reason` [[app/runtime.py:103-104]] [[app/runtime.py:120-125]]. The secret and stop-reason files are written with mode `0o600` [[app/runtime.py:128-132]] [[app/runtime.py:147-151]]. The idle timer reads the mtime of `last-activity` [[app/runtime.py:107-117]].

`remove_workspace_data` deletes that whole root, but only after checking that the root's parent is exactly the user's directory and that the root is not a symlink; otherwise it raises `ValueError` [[app/runtime.py:92-99]]. A test confirms only the selected workspace is removed [[tests/test_gateway.py:101-111]].

## Identity, secret and port

`start_workspace` derives three values from its arguments [[app/runtime.py:207-214]]:

- The container name is `oc-<slot_id>-<first 12 hex characters of the workspace id>`.
- The OpenCode password is `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, generated fresh on every start.
- The host port comes from `workspace_host_port(slot_id)`, the configured base (41000 by default) plus the slot id [[app/runtime.py:164-165]] [[app/config.py:58-58]].

Before launching, it runs `podman rm -f` on that name, because a crash may have left it behind, then clears any previous stop reason and persists the password with `write_workspace_secret` [[app/runtime.py:216-219]]. That file is how the gateway later learns the password; `read_workspace_secret` raises a "secret is missing" error if the file is absent [[app/runtime.py:154-161]]. See [The gateway proxy](wiki:gateway-proxy) for its use.

## Container flags

The `podman run -d` argument list is built inline [[app/runtime.py:221-248]].

| Concern | Flags |
|---|---|
| Reachability | `--publish 127.0.0.1:<port>:4096`, loopback only, with a comment that nothing outside the host can reach it directly [[app/runtime.py:225-227]] |
| Resources | `--memory`, `--cpus`, `--pids-limit` from settings, defaults 8g, 4.0 and 1024 [[app/runtime.py:228-230]] [[app/config.py:50-52]] |
| Privileges | `no-new-privileges`, `--cap-drop ALL`, and a user namespace mapping to uid and gid 10001 [[app/runtime.py:231-233]] |
| Filesystem | `--read-only` root with `tmpfs` mounts at `/tmp` (1g) and `~/.cache` (512m) [[app/runtime.py:234-236]] |
| State | The four directories bind-mounted read-write with the `Z` SELinux label [[app/runtime.py:237-240]] |
| Auth | `OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME=opencode` and `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` [[app/runtime.py:246-247]] |

Because the root filesystem is read-only, the `HOME` and `XDG_*` variables point at the writable mounts [[app/runtime.py:241-245]]. `OPENCODE_CORS` is added only when `settings.opencode_cors` is non-empty [[app/runtime.py:253-254]]. The image and the `serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096` command come last [[app/runtime.py:255-258]]. Every Podman call goes through `_run`, which applies a 90-second timeout and raises `RuntimeError` with stdout and stderr on a non-zero exit unless `check=False` [[app/runtime.py:25-40]].

## The managed provider policy

Administrators can restrict model providers through two comma-separated settings, `opencode_enabled_providers` and `opencode_disabled_providers`. A comment says they are applied as OpenCode managed settings to every workspace and take precedence over project config [[app/config.py:64-67]]. `Settings.enabled_provider_ids` and `Settings.disabled_provider_ids` parse them with `Settings._provider_ids`, which trims whitespace, drops blanks and duplicates, and keeps order [[app/config.py:77-93]].

`managed_opencode_config_path` turns that into a file [[app/runtime.py:66-89]]:

- It builds a JSON object with the OpenCode `$schema` and adds `enabled_providers` and/or `disabled_providers` only when non-empty. If nothing but the schema remains it returns `None` [[app/runtime.py:68-76]]. In that case the function does not touch an earlier file in the policy directory.
- Otherwise it writes `<data_root>/policy/opencode.json`. The file is the same for every workspace; its path contains no user or project [[app/runtime.py:78-80]].
- The write is atomic: it dumps to a temporary file in the same directory, sets mode `0o644`, then `replace`s the target [[app/runtime.py:81-88]]. A reader never sees a half-written policy.

`start_workspace` calls it on every start [[app/runtime.py:210-210]] and, when a path comes back, mounts it read-only at `/etc/opencode/opencode.json` [[app/runtime.py:249-252]]. Read-only is what makes the policy "immutable" from inside the container (the docstring uses that word [[app/runtime.py:67-67]]). Tests check de-duplication, file mode and the `:ro,Z` mount [[tests/test_gateway.py:18-53]]. A policy change applies to workspaces started afterwards. The code shown does not touch running containers.

## The readiness wait

After `run`, `start_workspace` calls `wait_workspace_ready` [[app/runtime.py:259-261]]. It computes a deadline from `workspace_ready_timeout_seconds` (45 by default) and builds a Basic header for user `opencode` [[app/runtime.py:169-171]] [[app/config.py:53-53]]. Each loop iteration does the following:

1. If the container is no longer running, it reads the last 80 log lines and raises "OpenCode container exited before becoming ready" with that text. A crashed container fails fast instead of waiting out the timeout [[app/runtime.py:175-178]].
2. It sends `GET /global/health` to `127.0.0.1:<host_port>` with a 2-second timeout. Any 2xx response ends the wait [[app/runtime.py:180-191]].
3. A non-2xx status or a connection error is remembered as `last_error`, the connection is closed, and it sleeps `workspace_ready_poll_interval_seconds`, 0.5 by default [[app/runtime.py:192-199]] [[app/config.py:54-54]].

When the deadline passes it raises a `RuntimeError` naming the timeout, the port and the last error [[app/runtime.py:201-204]]. A test with a fake connection covers the success path [[tests/test_gateway.py:155-173]].

If the wait raises, `start_workspace` force-removes the container and re-raises [[app/runtime.py:260-264]]. The secret file written earlier is not removed on that path in the code shown. On success it touches `last-activity`, so a new workspace does not look idle, and returns a `RuntimeResult` holding the container name, password and host port [[app/runtime.py:265-266]] [[app/runtime.py:18-22]].

guide.title: The gateway proxy
guide.purpose: Follow one browser request through workspace selection, credential swapping, streaming, WebSocket relay and widget injection.
guide.markdown:
The gateway is the reverse proxy that sits between the portal's public port and the per-workspace OpenCode containers. This page follows one request through it: which workspace is chosen, how the user's portal credentials are replaced, how the response is streamed or rewritten, and how WebSockets are relayed.

`app/main.py` imports `proxy_http`, `proxy_websocket` and `selected_workspace_for_request` from `app/gateway.py` [[app/main.py:16-16]]. The route handlers that call them are outside the excerpt shown for this page, so the sections below start where the gateway functions take over. For how the container and its port come to exist, see [Starting a workspace runtime](wiki:starting-a-workspace-runtime); for the slot a workspace holds, see [Slots and workspace leases](wiki:slots-and-workspace-leases).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant G as Gateway
    participant O as OpenCode container
    B->>G: request + portal session cookie
    G->>G: pick running workspace
    G->>G: read secret, build headers
    G->>O: request with Basic auth (127.0.0.1:port)
    O-->>G: response
    G-->>B: streamed body, or HTML with widget
```

## Choosing the workspace

`_find_selected_workspace` only considers workspaces that belong to the user and have status `RUNNING` [[app/gateway.py:80-83]]. The behaviour then depends on whether the client named one:

- With a selector, it matches either the workspace id or the container name, and answers 404 if nothing matches [[app/gateway.py:84-91]].
- Without one, it lists the user's running workspaces, newest first. Zero running gives 409 "No running workspace", and more than one gives 409 asking the caller to pick one. Exactly one is used implicitly [[app/gateway.py:93-101]].

`selected_workspace_for_request` takes the selector from the `x-opencode-workspace` header and falls back to the workspace cookie [[app/gateway.py:104-106]]. `selected_workspace_for_websocket` does the same for WebSockets [[app/gateway.py:109-111]]. Because the query always filters by `user.id`, a selector for someone else's workspace behaves like one that does not exist.

The backend address is derived from the slot: `_backend_http_url` raises 503 if the workspace has no slot, and otherwise targets `127.0.0.1` on `workspace_host_port(ws.slot_id)`, keeping the original path and query string [[app/gateway.py:114-120]]. `_backend_ws_url` builds the equivalent `ws://` URL [[app/gateway.py:123-129]].

## Swapping credentials

The browser holds a portal session, but OpenCode expects Basic Auth. `_forward_headers` builds the outgoing header set:

- It drops hop-by-hop headers plus `host`, `authorization` and `content-length` [[app/gateway.py:56-57]].
- It drops `x-opencode-workspace`, so a client-controlled routing header never reaches OpenCode [[app/gateway.py:58-61]].
- It removes the portal's session and workspace cookies through `_clean_cookie_header` and keeps any other cookies [[app/gateway.py:36-48]] [[app/gateway.py:62-68]].
- It sets `authorization` from `_basic_auth`, which encodes the user name `opencode` with the workspace secret [[app/gateway.py:31-33]] [[app/gateway.py:69-69]].
- It forces `accept-encoding: identity` [[app/gateway.py:70-70]]. This keeps response bodies uncompressed so HTML can be edited later. The widget code also removes any upstream `content-encoding` when it rewrites a page [[app/gateway.py:195-196]].

A test covers the stripping of session, routing and host headers and the cookie filtering [[tests/test_gateway.py:56-73]], and another covers the identity encoding [[tests/test_gateway.py:204-208]].

## Forwarding an HTTP request

`proxy_http` does the following:

1. Resolves the workspace, records activity with `touch_workspace_activity`, reads the workspace secret and reads the whole request body [[app/gateway.py:133-138]].
2. Opens an `httpx.AsyncClient` that does not follow redirects, has no timeout and ignores proxy environment variables, and sends the request with `stream=True` [[app/gateway.py:140-145]].
3. Converts any `httpx.HTTPError` into a 502 that names the exception type [[app/gateway.py:146-152]].

The recorded activity is what idle reclamation later reads; see [Startup, reconciliation and idle reclamation](wiki:startup-reconciliation-and-idle-reclamation).

The response takes one of two paths. A 200 response with a `text/html` content type is read fully, decoded with the upstream charset (default UTF-8), passed through `inject_portal_widget` and returned as a plain `Response` [[app/gateway.py:154-166]]. Everything else is streamed chunk by chunk. Each chunk touches the activity file again, and a background task closes the upstream response and client when streaming ends [[app/gateway.py:167-181]].

Headers are copied from the raw upstream list so duplicates such as `Set-Cookie` survive. Hop-by-hop headers and `content-length` are skipped, since the body length may change [[app/gateway.py:183-190]]. A `Location` header that starts with the loopback backend origin is rewritten to `settings.control_plane_url`, so the browser never sees `127.0.0.1` [[app/gateway.py:197-201]].

## Relaying a WebSocket

`proxy_websocket` cannot use the cookie-based dependency that HTTP routes use, so it authenticates itself. It reads the session cookie, accepts a `Bearer` token in the `Authorization` header when there is no cookie, and calls `load_user_from_token`. An unauthenticated socket is closed with code 4401 [[app/gateway.py:207-214]].

If workspace selection fails, the code checks whether the selector names a stopped workspace whose stop reason is `idle`. If so, it closes with code 4409 and a message pointing back to the dashboard. Otherwise the original error is re-raised [[app/gateway.py:216-236]].

When selection succeeds, the gateway connects to the container first, with a 15 second open timeout, no message size limit and no proxy. Only after that does it accept the browser's socket [[app/gateway.py:237-249]]. Two coroutines then pump messages:

- Client to upstream: text and binary frames are forwarded, and the loop stops on a disconnect message [[app/gateway.py:251-262]].
- Upstream to client: frames are forwarded with the matching text or bytes call [[app/gateway.py:264-270]].

Every frame in either direction counts as activity [[app/gateway.py:258-266]]. `asyncio.wait` returns when either pump finishes. The other is cancelled, and an exception from the finished one is re-raised [[app/gateway.py:272-285]]. Any exception ends in a close with code 1011 [[app/gateway.py:286-290]].

## Injecting the portal widget

`inject_portal_widget` leaves a page unchanged if it already contains `id="oc-mu-portal"`. Otherwise it inserts `portal_markup` before the last `</body>`, found case-insensitively, or appends it when there is none [[app/portal.py:103-111]]. Tests check both the placement and that injecting twice leaves one widget [[tests/test_gateway.py:176-193]].

`portal_markup` escapes the project slug and builds a `<details>` menu with Dashboard, Stop workspace and Logout controls. It also links `/_portal/widget.css` and `/_portal/widget.js` [[app/portal.py:86-100]]. The script polls `/_portal/status` every 30 seconds. It redirects to `/login` on a 401 and to the dashboard when the workspace is not running. It adds `reason=idle` when the workspace stopped for inactivity [[app/portal.py:57-81]]. The server routes behind those `/_portal/` URLs are not part of the files shown here.

guide.title: Startup, reconciliation and idle reclamation
guide.purpose: Understand how the app prepares the database at startup and keeps database leases in line with real containers over time.
guide.markdown:
The database and the containers can disagree: a crash, an upgrade or a manual `podman` command can leave a workspace marked running with no usable container. This page covers how the app prepares the database at startup, and how it keeps leases in line with reality afterwards, both by reconciling stale runtimes and by reclaiming idle ones.

## The startup sequence

The FastAPI `lifespan` context manager does all start-up work before the app serves requests. The order matters, and the comments in the code explain several of the steps [[app/main.py:281-297]].

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["validate_auth"] --> B["drop_legacy_workspace_constraint"]
    B --> C["migrate_user_auth_schema"]
    C --> D["Base.metadata.create_all"]
    D --> E["_seed_slots"]
    E --> F["create data and Traefik dirs"]
    F --> G["cleanup_legacy_workspace_routes"]
    G --> H["_reconcile_workspace_runtimes"]
    H --> I["_dedupe_active_workspaces"]
    I --> J["ensure_active_workspace_index"]
    J --> K{"idle timeout > 0?"}
    K -- yes --> L["start _idle_reaper_loop"]
    K -- no --> M["serve"]
    L --> M
```

### Schema preparation

There is no migration framework. `app/migrations.py` holds idempotent functions that run on every start.

- `drop_legacy_workspace_constraint` removes the old `uq_activeish_workspace` constraint on PostgreSQL, using `IF EXISTS` so a fresh database is safe. On SQLite it only logs that it skips the drop [[app/migrations.py:83-92]]. It runs before `create_all` so the old rule cannot conflict with the newer one [[app/main.py:282-288]].
- `migrate_user_auth_schema` returns immediately if there is no `users` table, because `create_all` will build it from the current model [[app/migrations.py:21-23]]. Otherwise it adds the role, provider and OIDC columns. On PostgreSQL it uses `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` and drops `NOT NULL` on `password_hash`. On SQLite it adds only the columns that are missing. Other dialects log a warning and are skipped [[app/migrations.py:25-56]].
- It then backfills `developer` and `local` for empty values, and promotes the oldest user to `admin` only if no admin exists [[app/migrations.py:58-66]]. On PostgreSQL it adds defaults and `NOT NULL`, and it creates a partial unique index on the OIDC issuer and subject [[app/migrations.py:67-79]]. See [Authentication and roles](wiki:authentication-and-roles) for what those roles mean.
- `ensure_active_workspace_index` creates the unique index `uq_active_workspace` on `(user_id, project_slug)`, limited to rows in `STARTING`, `RUNNING` or `STOPPING`. It supports only PostgreSQL and SQLite [[app/migrations.py:95-109]]. This index is the database guarantee behind [Slots and workspace leases](wiki:slots-and-workspace-leases).

`_seed_slots` inserts any slot ids from 1 to `settings.max_slots` that are missing. It never deletes existing ones [[app/main.py:72-78]].

The app also removes v5 per-workspace Traefik files with `cleanup_legacy_workspace_routes`, which deletes `workspace-*.yml` in the dynamic directory [[app/traefik.py:8-14]] [[app/main.py:292-294]].

### Why reconcile and dedupe come before the index

A unique partial index cannot be built over rows that already violate it. So `_dedupe_active_workspaces` runs first. For each user and project it keeps the newest active row and releases the rest [[app/main.py:145-167]]. The index is created only afterwards [[app/main.py:295-297]].

## Reconciling leases with containers

`_workspace_runtime_usable` is the test for "this running workspace is real". All of these must hold [[app/main.py:110-118]]:

- the status is `RUNNING`
- it has a slot and a container name
- the secret file exists
- `container_running` is true
- `container_has_workspace_port` is true

The last check runs `podman port` for `4096/tcp` and requires a line equal to `127.0.0.1:` plus the slot's host port. A container that exists but is bound to the wrong port therefore counts as stale [[app/runtime.py:282-290]].

`_reconcile_workspace_runtimes` loads every workspace in `STARTING`, `RUNNING` or `STOPPING` and releases each one that is not usable, with reason `recycle`. It returns the number released [[app/main.py:121-143]]. A `STARTING` workspace fails the usability test because it is not `RUNNING`, and the function does not skip it. At startup that is what clears leases left by a crash mid-start. The code shown does not say how this interacts with a start that is genuinely in progress while the periodic pass runs.

`_release_workspace` is the single path for freeing a lease. It marks the workspace `STOPPING` and commits, then stops the container. It then clears `in_use` and `workspace_id` on the slot, sets the workspace to `STOPPED`, clears `container_name` and `slot_id`, writes the stop reason and commits [[app/main.py:84-105]].

## Idle reclamation

Activity is a file. `touch_workspace_activity` creates or touches a marker file, and `workspace_last_activity` returns its mtime in UTC, or `None` if it does not exist [[app/runtime.py:107-117]]. The gateway touches it on every proxied exchange (see [The gateway proxy](wiki:gateway-proxy)). Starting or opening a workspace also touches it [[app/main.py:678-678]] [[app/main.py:849-849]].

`_reap_idle_workspaces` does nothing when `workspace_idle_timeout_minutes` is zero or negative [[app/main.py:241-243]]. Otherwise it computes a cutoff and checks each `RUNNING` workspace [[app/main.py:245-250]]. Its last activity is the marker mtime, falling back to `created_at`. A naive timestamp is treated as UTC. A workspace at or before the cutoff is released with reason `idle` [[app/main.py:251-264]]. The stop reason is written to a `stop-reason` file [[app/runtime.py:128-132]].

That reason is what lets the system explain itself. When a later request cannot find a running workspace, `_idle_timeout_response` checks for a stopped workspace whose reason is `idle`. A browser navigation is redirected to `/dashboard?reason=idle`, and an API call gets a 409 with code `workspace_idle_timeout` [[app/main.py:877-916]].

### The background loop

`_idle_reaper_loop` sleeps first, using the larger of 5 seconds and `workspace_reaper_interval_seconds`. It then runs reconciliation and reaping, each in a worker thread via `asyncio.to_thread` so blocking Podman and database calls do not stall the event loop. Cancellation is re-raised, and any other exception is logged so the loop keeps running [[app/main.py:267-277]].

`lifespan` starts the loop as a named task only when the timeout is positive. On shutdown it cancels the task and awaits it [[app/main.py:298-306]]. Both functions open their own session with `SessionLocal` rather than using the request-scoped `get_db` dependency [[app/main.py:124-124]] [[app/main.py:247-247]] [[app/db.py:15-23]].

guide.title: Admin console and engine updates
guide.purpose: See how administrators manage users safely and how the OpenCode engine image is updated without interrupting running workspaces.
guide.markdown:
This page covers the two administrator tools in the portal: the user console, whose API refuses changes that would lock everyone out, and the system console, which builds, tests and activates a new OpenCode engine image without touching running workspaces. For how admins are identified in the first place, see [Authentication and roles](wiki:authentication-and-roles).

## Who can reach it

Every admin page and API route in `app/main.py` takes `admin: User = Depends(require_admin)`, for example the two HTML pages [[app/main.py:501-508]] and the update trigger [[app/main.py:533-537]]. `require_admin` lives in `app/security.py`, which is not part of this page's source, so its exact check is not described here. The HTML pages (`admin_users_page_html`, `admin_system_page_html`) are static shells: they render the header and empty containers, then fetch data from the JSON endpoints in the browser [[app/ui.py:189-232]] [[app/ui.py:235-268]].

## Managing users safely

The main hazard is an administrator removing the last way to administer the system. Three mechanisms guard against it.

### Last-admin protection

`_protect_last_admin` raises HTTP 409 when an action removes admin access from a target who is currently an enabled admin and the count of enabled admins is 1 or less [[app/main.py:236-238]]. The count is `_enabled_admin_count`: users with the admin role and `is_active` true [[app/main.py:191-192]]. A disabled admin is therefore not counted, and demoting one is allowed.

A count followed by a write is a race: two requests could each see "another admin remains" and both proceed. `_lock_users_for_admin_mutation` closes this on PostgreSQL by taking `LOCK TABLE users IN SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE MODE`, so concurrent admin mutations are serialized. On other database dialects it does nothing [[app/main.py:184-188]]. It is called first in the role, status and delete handlers [[app/main.py:568-568]] [[app/main.py:586-586]] [[app/main.py:631-631]].

### Per-action rules

| Action | Route handler | Refused when |
|---|---|---|
| Change role | `admin_change_role` | the target is the caller and the new role is not admin; or it would remove the last enabled admin [[app/main.py:570-572]] |
| Enable or disable | `admin_change_status` | the caller disables their own account; or it would disable the last enabled admin [[app/main.py:588-590]] |
| Delete | `admin_delete_user` | the target is the caller; is not a local account; is the last enabled admin; or has any workspace history [[app/main.py:633-640]] |
| Reset password | `admin_reset_password` | the account is not local [[app/main.py:617-619]] |

Details worth noting:

- Disabling a user who is currently active first releases all their active workspaces with reason `"admin"`, so their slots are freed before the flag flips [[app/main.py:591-593]]. See [Slots and workspace leases](wiki:slots-and-workspace-leases) for what releasing means.
- Deletion is limited to accounts with no workspace rows at all. The message tells the admin to disable the account instead [[app/main.py:638-640]]. OIDC accounts are never deleted, only disabled [[app/main.py:635-636]].
- Stopping a user's workspaces and resetting a password do not take the table lock [[app/main.py:599-622]].
- The role payload is validated at the API boundary: `AdminRoleUpdate.role` must match `admin` or `developer`, and `AdminPasswordReset.password` has the same 12 to 256 character bounds as registration [[app/schemas.py:33-42]].

The list endpoint builds each row with `_admin_user_payload`, which includes a `can_delete` flag computed from the same rules (local, not self, no history) [[app/main.py:195-226]]. It does not include the last-admin check, so the server-side guard remains the real enforcement. The browser UI hides the role selector and the disable button for the caller's own row, and shows Delete only when `can_delete` is true [[app/ui.py:219-219]].

## Updating the OpenCode engine

Workspaces run from a container image. An update builds a candidate image, verifies it, and only then moves the live tag. It is started from `admin_opencode_update`, which returns HTTP 202 immediately [[app/main.py:533-543]].

### Starting an update

`start_update` validates the version, claims the single update slot under `_LOCK`, resets `_STATE`, and starts `_perform_update` in a daemon thread [[app/opencode_update.py:195-210]]. If the state is already `queued`, `building`, `testing` or `activating`, it raises `RuntimeError`, which the route maps to 409. A bad version raises `ValueError`, mapped to 422 [[app/opencode_update.py:198-199]] [[app/main.py:540-543]].

Validation happens twice on the server side. `OpenCodeUpdateRequest.version` has a length and regex constraint [[app/schemas.py:45-46]], and `validate_version` checks a semantic-version pattern (`_SEMVER`, defined outside the shown excerpt) and returns the stripped value [[app/opencode_update.py:46-50]]. The page also checks in JavaScript before posting [[app/ui.py:266-266]].

### The worker

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> building
    building --> testing
    testing --> activating
    activating --> success
    building --> error
    testing --> error
    activating --> error
```

`_perform_update` goes through these stages, recording each in `_STATE` [[app/opencode_update.py:132-192]]:

1. **Build.** `podman build` with `OPENCODE_VERSION` as a build argument, tagged `localhost/opencode-workspace:<version>` (a `+` in the version becomes `_` in the tag), using `Containerfile.workspace` [[app/opencode_update.py:133-155]].
2. **Smoke test.** It runs the candidate with `--version`, extracts a version number from the last output line, and fails unless it equals the requested version [[app/opencode_update.py:160-165]].
3. **Activate.** It tags the candidate as `settings.workspace_image`, then calls `_persist_version` [[app/opencode_update.py:171-173]].

Because the retag happens only after the smoke test passes, a failed build or mismatched version leaves the live image alone. The error handler says so in its message and keeps the candidate tag for inspection [[app/opencode_update.py:181-188]].

`_persist_version` rewrites the `OPENCODE_VERSION=` line in the control-plane env file, or appends one, sets mode `0600`, and updates `settings.opencode_version` in memory [[app/opencode_update.py:114-129]]. The file's path (`_CONFIG_FILE`) is defined outside the shown lines.

### Running workspaces are not interrupted

Nothing in the worker stops or restarts a container. On success it logs that existing workspaces are unchanged and must be restarted to use the new image [[app/opencode_update.py:174-174]], and the system page states the same policy [[app/ui.py:245-245]] [[app/ui.py:251-251]]. New workspaces pick up the new image when they start; how the image is used at start-up is covered in [Starting a workspace runtime](wiki:starting-a-workspace-runtime).

### Observing progress

State lives in a process-wide `_STATE` guarded by `_LOCK`, so it is per process and lost on restart. The status route returns it [[app/main.py:528-530]]. `system_snapshot` combines configured and installed versions, the image name, the registry URL and the update status; the latest upstream version is queried only when `check_latest` is true [[app/opencode_update.py:218-234]]. The system endpoint passes `check_latest=False` [[app/main.py:511-516]], and a separate route does the registry lookup, turning failures into 502 [[app/main.py:519-525]].

In the browser, `renderUpdate` disables the buttons while an update runs and polls the status route every 1.2 seconds until it finishes, then reloads the system state [[app/ui.py:262-262]].

guide.title: Installation, versioning and releases
guide.purpose: Learn how a release is versioned and packaged, and what the installer sets up and preserves across upgrades.
guide.markdown:
This page follows a release from its version number, through the archive that `scripts/package-release.sh` builds, to what `scripts/install.sh` does on a host, including what it keeps when you run it again to upgrade.

## One version number

The application version is a single string in `app/version.py`, and its docstring calls the module the single source of truth [[app/version.py:1-8]]. `app/__init__.py` re-exports it, so code can read `app.__version__` [[app/__init__.py:3-5]]. `tests/test_version.py` checks that the login and registration pages contain `v{__version__}` [[tests/test_version.py:18-20]]. The installer reads the same line with `sed` rather than calling `scripts/version.py`, and aborts if it cannot find it [[scripts/install.sh:56-58]].

### Changing it with `scripts/version.py`

The script edits `app/version.py` in place. Two regular expressions define the format: strict `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with no leading zeros, and the `__version__ = "..."` assignment line [[scripts/version.py:20-21]].

- `read_version` finds the assignment, fails with `SystemExit` if it is missing, and also fails if the value is not valid semver [[scripts/version.py:24-32]].
- `write_version` validates the new value and replaces the assignment with a single-substitution regex. It aborts unless exactly one replacement happened [[scripts/version.py:41-47]].
- `bump` increments one component and zeroes the lower ones; any part other than `major` or `minor` falls through to patch [[scripts/version.py:50-56]]. The command line restricts the choice to the three names, so the fall-through is not reachable from the CLI [[scripts/version.py:66-66]].
- `main` handles `show`, `set <version>` and `bump <part>`, defaults to `show` when no subcommand is given, and prints `old -> new` after a write [[scripts/version.py:59-79]].

Pre-release or build suffixes such as `1.2.3-rc1` are rejected here. The OpenCode engine version is a separate setting, handled in [Admin console and engine updates](wiki:admin-console-and-engine-updates).

### The tests that pin it

`test_application_version_is_semver` compares `__version__` against a literal string, so a bump through `scripts/version.py` must be accompanied by an edit to that test [[tests/test_version.py:13-15]]. `test_version_cli_show` runs the script in a subprocess and asserts that its trimmed output equals `__version__`, which keeps the CLI and the package from drifting [[tests/test_version.py:23-32]].

## Packaging a release

`scripts/package-release.sh` asks `scripts/version.py show` for the version and names the release `opencode-multiuser-<version>` [[scripts/package-release.sh:6-7]]. It requires `rsync` and `zip` [[scripts/package-release.sh:12-13]]. It stages a copy of the repository into a temporary directory that is removed on exit [[scripts/package-release.sh:9-10]], leaving out `.git`, virtualenvs, caches, build output and `dist` [[scripts/package-release.sh:16-25]]. Then it zips the staged folder into the output directory (default `dist`) and writes a `.sha256` file next to it [[scripts/package-release.sh:27-35]]. It prints both paths [[scripts/package-release.sh:37-38]].

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["app/version.py"] --> B["scripts/version.py show"]
    B --> C["package-release.sh"]
    C --> D["name-version.zip"]
    C --> E["name-version.zip.sha256"]
    D --> F["install.sh from extracted tree"]
```

## What the installer does

`scripts/install.sh` runs from an extracted release tree [[scripts/install.sh:22-22]]. It is written to be re-run, so most of its logic is about deciding which value wins: the environment, the saved file, or a default.

### Preflight

1. **Complete tree.** It refuses to continue unless a list of files, including `app/portal.py`, `app/opencode_update.py`, `app/version.py` and `uv.lock`, exists, to avoid a partial upgrade [[scripts/install.sh:24-32]].
2. **Python 3.11+.** It uses `PYTHON_BIN` if set, otherwise tries `python3.13`, `python3.12`, `python3.11`, then `python3`, and accepts the first that is at least 3.11 [[scripts/install.sh:34-53]].
3. **systemd user session.** It needs the runtime directory and the user bus socket, and `systemctl --user` must work [[scripts/install.sh:60-85]].
4. **cgroup delegation.** `cpu`, `memory` and `pids` controllers must be delegated to the user manager. If the controllers file cannot be read, it only warns [[scripts/install.sh:87-114]].
5. **Port.** If `ss` is available and `CONTROL_PLANE_PORT` is already in use, it stops [[scripts/install.sh:168-175]]. The control-plane service is stopped just before this check so a previous install does not block itself [[scripts/install.sh:166-166]].

`scripts/check-host.sh` is the read-only counterpart for the same host checks. It prints the runtime directory, user bus, cgroup controllers and Podman's cgroup settings, and changes nothing [[scripts/check-host.sh:3-16]].

### Settings that survive an upgrade

At the top, the script records whether each of `BASE_DOMAIN`, `OPENCODE_VERSION`, the provider lists, `CONTROL_PLANE_PORT`, `DATA_ROOT` and `TRAEFIK_DYNAMIC_DIR` was set explicitly, using `${VAR+x}` [[scripts/install.sh:4-17]]. If `control-plane.env` already exists, each value that was not explicit is read back from it [[scripts/install.sh:123-153]]. Defaults for `DATA_ROOT` and the Traefik directory apply only afterwards, both must be absolute, and `%h` is expanded to `$HOME` [[scripts/install.sh:155-162]].

The env file itself has two paths:

- **Fresh install.** It generates a random `JWT_SECRET`, writes the full file with a PostgreSQL URL, and sets mode `600` [[scripts/install.sh:204-258]]. The database password is generated once into `postgres.env` and reused on later runs [[scripts/install.sh:196-202]].
- **Upgrade.** Existing values are left alone; each missing key is appended with its default via `grep -q ... || echo ... >>` [[scripts/install.sh:259-297]]. Explicit `DATA_ROOT` and `TRAEFIK_DYNAMIC_DIR` overrides are then written over the saved ones [[scripts/install.sh:298-303]].

Two migrations adjust the public URL: a legacy `http://code.example.com` default is rewritten, and an `https://` URL is rewritten to HTTP when `TRAEFIK_TLS` is not `true` [[scripts/install.sh:305-318]]. An explicit `OPENCODE_VERSION` or provider-policy override becomes the new saved value [[scripts/install.sh:321-343]]. The image build later reads the effective value back from the file [[scripts/install.sh:368-371]]; the admin update flow described in [Admin console and engine updates](wiki:admin-console-and-engine-updates) also maintains that setting.

### Copying, building and starting

The app is copied to `~/opt/opencode-multiuser` with `rsync -a --delete`, excluding `.venv` and `.pytest_cache`, and the copy is verified again for the key files [[scripts/install.sh:116-121]] [[scripts/install.sh:177-184]]. Quadlet files go to `~/.config/containers/systemd`, with the Traefik file's placeholders for its dynamic and state directories substituted. The control-plane unit and `traefik.yml` are copied too [[scripts/install.sh:185-194]]. The Traefik route file is rendered from a template, and old `workspace-*.yml` routes are deleted, since every workspace now goes through the gateway [[scripts/install.sh:350-358]].

The virtualenv is deleted and recreated on every run, then dependencies come from `uv sync --frozen --no-dev` [[scripts/install.sh:360-366]]. The workspace image is built as `localhost/opencode-workspace:latest` using the effective saved OpenCode version, and the PostgreSQL and Traefik images are pulled [[scripts/install.sh:368-373]]. Finally it starts the network, PostgreSQL and Traefik units, then enables and restarts the control plane [[scripts/install.sh:375-379]].

## Cleaning up stuck containers

`scripts/reset-orphans.sh` force-removes containers whose names match `oc-<digits>-<hex>`, so fixed services such as PostgreSQL and Traefik are untouched [[scripts/reset-orphans.sh:3-4]]. It only touches Podman; it does not edit the database. How the app reconciles leases with real containers is covered in [Startup, reconciliation and idle reclamation](wiki:startup-reconciliation-and-idle-reclamation).
